title: The last kindness
hook: mourners shovel earth into the grave themselves

segments.voice: Yesterday, the funeral, and El Male Rachamim. Your line: god full of mercy. Today, the graveside, a little longer.

"And Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him." That's how Genesis, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, closes the story of Abraham. Two brothers who grew up apart, one sent away into the wilderness as a boy, stand at the same grave. The text doesn't say they made peace. It says they buried their father. Once the prayers are said, the shovel doesn't stay with the cemetery workers. The daughter picks it up. Then the brother. Then the old friend from work. Earth lands on a plain wooden lid, slow and heavy and hard to watch. The tradition calls it a kindness.
screen: `ISAAC AND ISHMAEL AT ONE GRAVE.` → `THE MOURNERS TAKE THE SHOVEL.` → `EARTH ON PLAIN WOOD.`

segments.voice: First, the sons at the grave. Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham. A generation later, Genesis says the same of Isaac: his sons Esau and Jacob bury him, two more brothers with a hard history. Whatever lay between them, the burial was theirs to do. Second, the name. Earlier this week you met Rashi's phrase for care of the dead: chesed shel emet, the kindness of truth, a kindness the one who receives it can never repay. Filling the grave is its last act, and the tradition gives it to the people who loved the person, not only to strangers. It makes the death real. Nobody leaves the cemetery thinking it was a dream. Third, the small customs. In some communities the first scoops are taken with the back of the blade, so it doesn't look like ordinary digging. And nobody hands the shovel over. You push it back into the mound and step away, and the next person picks it up on their own. Some explain the back of the shovel as reluctance, and putting it down as not handing grief from one person to the next. Communities give different reasons, and keep the custom anyway. Fourth, the circle. Friends and neighbors take a turn too, because the work is shared. The person in the grave will never know who lifted the earth. No one is left to say thank you, and the shovel goes round anyway.
screen: `BROTHERS AT ONE GRAVE.` · `THE KINDNESS OF TRUTH.` · `NOT HANDED, PUT DOWN.` · `NO ONE LEFT TO THANK YOU.` · then, large: `THE LAST KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a kindness you've been putting off, not because it's big but because it's hard: a call to someone who is ill, an awkward visit. Picture picking it up the way a mourner takes the shovel, once, with both hands, without waiting to be handed it; if you pray, hold that person in your prayer. And if the grief you're carrying is your own and it feels like too much, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
The last kindness. Chesed shel emet, the kindness of truth: care for the dead, who can never repay it. Today's word.
Your line: the last kindness. The work belongs to the people who loved them. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: At a Jewish burial, after the prayers, mourners and friends take turns placing earth into the grave themselves; in some communities the shovel is put back into the earth rather than handed from person to person.

chat.says: At my friend's Jewish funeral, why did the family shovel the dirt in themselves?
options: Burying is a kindness the dead can't repay, so the people who loved them do it.
Cemeteries ask families to do it, mostly to keep the cost of burial down.
It's only for close family, to show who inherits from the one who died.
chat.meaning: Filling the grave is chesed shel emet, the kindness of truth: care for someone who can never repay it, kept in the hands of those who loved them.

notes: Genesis 25:9 fragment quoted as JPS 1917; confirm exact wording (KJV identical). Genesis 35:29 (Esau and Jacob bury Isaac) paraphrased.
Rashi on Genesis 47:29 paraphrased: kindness done with the dead is true kindness, since one does not expect repayment. Confirm.

Customs kept to 'some communities': using the back of the shovel for the first scoops, and returning the shovel to the earth rather than handing it on. Explanations given as 'some explain'. Confirm both are fair to describe.
